subtype: Approach: finding out the topics and format first [Thinking]
passage: In the small town's government school, the headmaster pinned a notice on the board: inter-school quiz, next month. Sunil read it twice. Then, instead of rushing off to memorise everything, he asked Gargi Ma'am, "What subjects will it cover, and how are the rounds?" She checked the circular. "Science, sports and general knowledge, and there are buzzer rounds." Sunil sat down with a pencil. "So fast recall matters, and I should read about all three. Not history or maths so much." He listed sports records first, then science facts, and decided to practise answering aloud quickly, as if a buzzer had sounded.

qa.q: Which subjects would the quiz cover?
qa.a: The quiz would cover science, sports and general knowledge.

qa.q: How does Sunil feel about the quiz once he knows about the buzzer rounds?
qa.a: Sunil feels focused and determined; he plans to practise answering aloud quickly, as if a buzzer had sounded, because fast recall matters.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sunil use to prepare, and why?
qa.a: Sunil could join a partner for practice rounds or read widely from newspapers. Practice with another person shows how quickly he actually answers.

qa.q: How does Gargi Ma'am help Sunil?
qa.a: Gargi Ma'am checked the circular and gave the details, so the teacher helps Sunil aim his study at the right topics.

grounding: A boy learns the quiz covers general knowledge, science and sports with buzzer rounds, so knowing the format tells him what to prepare and how quickly to answer.

subtype: Approach: finding out the topics and format first [Thinking]
passage: When Mateo's school in Valencia signed up for the inter-school quiz, he did not start reading the encyclopaedia. He went to the teacher first. "What will the rounds be?" She showed him the letter: general knowledge, science, sports, and two buzzer rounds where the fastest hand wins. Mateo thought it through on the way home with his friend Emil. "So three subjects. We don't need history or maths. And buzzer rounds mean we have to be quick, not just right." That evening he made three piles of books and practised with Emil, one reading, one slapping the kitchen table like a buzzer, until they got faster.

qa.q: What were the subjects in the quiz?
qa.a: General knowledge, science and sports, with two buzzer rounds.

qa.q: How did Mateo feel once he knew the format?
qa.a: He felt clear and confident, because he now knew exactly what to prepare and what to skip.

qa.q: What else could Mateo find out about the quiz, and why?
qa.a: He could ask how many points each round gives, because that would tell him where to spend the most time.

qa.q: How does Mateo's plan look to Emil?
qa.a: Emil gets a clear, fun way to practise with him, slapping the table as a buzzer, so it feels like a game.

grounding: It shows a boy finding out a quiz's topics and buzzer format first so he knows what to prepare and how fast to answer.

subtype: Approach: finding out the topics and format first [Thinking]
passage: In the school library, Nilesh stood at the librarian's desk with the quiz notice. "Hafsa ma'am, what kind of questions come in the district quiz?" She pulled out last year's booklet. "General knowledge, science, sports. The final has a buzzer round." Nilesh read the booklet slowly. "So no geography round. And buzzer means speed. I can't just know it; I have to know it fast." He borrowed the booklet and a sports book. In the reading corner, he made a timetable: science on Mondays and Thursdays, sports on Tuesdays and Fridays, GK every day, and five minutes of buzzer practice with a friend at the end.

qa.q: What did Hafsa ma'am pull out for Nilesh?
qa.a: She pulled out last year's booklet.

qa.q: What was Nilesh thinking as he read the booklet slowly?
qa.a: He was working out what to study and what to skip, and he seemed focused and a little relieved to have a clear target.

qa.q: What else could Nilesh try to prepare for the buzzer round?
qa.a: He could practise with a timer, answering old questions within a few seconds, to build real speed.

qa.q: How does the question look to Hafsa ma'am?
qa.a: Hafsa ma'am sees a student preparing sensibly and is happy to lend him last year's booklet.

grounding: It shows a boy learning the quiz topics and buzzer format first so he knows what to study and how quickly he must answer.
